summary.title: A Gentle Introduction to Graph Neural Networks
summary.one_liner: You learn how graphs are represented for neural networks (nodes, edges, global context, adjacency lists) and how message passing GNN layers, pooling and graph-level, node-level and edge-level predictions fit together.
keywords: how do neural networks work on graphs
takeaways: Graphs are represented as node, edge, and global feature matrices plus connectivity, and adjacency lists are a memory-efficient, permutation-friendly alternative to adjacency matrices.
Prediction tasks on graphs come in three levels: graph-level, node-level, and edge-level, and pooling routes information between nodes, edges and the global attribute.
Message passing GNN layers gather neighbor messages, aggregate them (e.g. sum), and update embeddings; stacking k layers lets a node see information k steps away.

Long-range information flow can be improved with a global context vector (master node), and design choices like depth, embedding size, aggregation type and which attributes update are explored empirically in an interactive playground on an odor-prediction task.
summary.summary: This Distill article introduces graph neural networks by first showing how graphs describe data such as images, text, molecules, social networks and citation networks. It then explains how to encode graphs for neural networks using feature matrices and adjacency lists, and how to perform graph-, node- and edge-level predictions via pooling. The author builds up from a simple per-attribute GNN to message passing layers and global-context variants. An interactive playground lets readers vary GNN design choices on a molecular odor classification task.
